claims.text: The initial eutectic HEA consists of a disordered FCC matrix and an ordered B2 phase.
The homogenized initial state has planar phase boundaries and minimal short-range chemical ordering.
Intermediate aging causes short-range LCOs to coalesce into coherent or semi-coherent B2 precipitates.
The resulting B2 ordered domains have high anti-phase-boundary energy.
High APB energy makes the ordered domains strong obstacles to dislocation motion.
Dislocations encountering the B2 domains must either bow around them by an Orowan mechanism or reach a high stress to shear them.
Intermediate aging changes phase boundaries from planar to undulated or roughened morphologies.
Roughened phase boundaries suppress cross-slip and restrict dislocation transmission.
The combined ordered-domain barriers and phase-boundary roughening cause a dramatic loss of ductility at intermediate aging temperatures.
At higher temperatures, thermal activation overcomes the APB-related barrier and enables dislocations to shear the ordered domains.
Higher temperature facilitates cross-slip and restores phase-boundary mobility.
The recovery of dislocation shearing, cross-slip, and phase-boundary mobility restores ductility at higher temperatures.
Ductility should vary non-monotonically with aging temperature, progressing from high ductility to near-zero ductility and then recovering.
The relevant aging window permits LCO evolution but not significant grain coarsening or impurity segregation.
The embrittlement regime lies between LCO coalescence into precipitates and the onset of thermally activated shearing, before grain coarsening occurs.
The location of the transient embrittlement window depends on composition-dependent APB energy and LCO-evolution kinetics.
Observation of easy B2 shearing without significant APB formation during the embrittlement regime would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Planar phase boundaries with unimpeded dislocation transmission during the embrittlement regime would falsify the proposed phase-boundary mechanism.
